content.overview: Dew point connects air moisture to surface condensation risk. Lights-off cooling, cold surfaces and moisture release can create local saturation even when room-average RH is below 100%.

vocabulary.definition: The temperature at which air with a given moisture content becomes saturated.
The possibility that a surface reaches or falls below dew-point temperature and water condenses.
A system change such as lights-off, irrigation, cooling start or dehumidifier cycling that alters environmental load.

sections.title: Surface temperature matters
sections.body: A leaf, wall, duct or pipe approaching the dew point can condense moisture even while bulk room RH remains lower than 100%.

sections.title: Lights-off can increase condensation risk
sections.body: Cooling air and surfaces while crop moisture remains high can quickly raise RH and reduce the margin to dew point. Review transition timing rather than daily averages alone.

sections.title: Dehumidification must match the moisture event
sections.body: Trend system response across irrigation, lights-off and crop-load changes to determine whether removal capacity and sequencing keep pace with the actual moisture load.

workedExamples: A canopy cools rapidly at lights-off while moisture remains high; surface temperatures approach dew point before the dehumidification sequence catches up.
commonMistakes: Using RH alone to judge condensation risk.
Treating a dew-point calculation as proof that condensation occurred without observing the surface state.
content.practicalApplication: Review a lights-off trend and identify when temperature, RH and dew-point margin suggest the highest condensation risk.
content.summary: Dew point is a surface-risk concept best used with trend timing and representative temperature measurements.
